190.title: Thou hast searched me (Psalm 138 [139])
190.hook: you knit me in my mother's womb, and there's nowhere God is not
190.tomorrow: let every spirit praise the Lord
190.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 138 [139] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and a verse of it shapes the traditional entrance chant of Easter Sunday; some pray its closing lines before an examination of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon, remembering Sion: exiles weeping, and rage handed to God. Your line was even anger can be prayed. Today, a psalm about being seen all the way through.

Some rooms in a life stay locked. A thing done at nineteen. A thought never said out loud. The self that shows up at two in the morning. People let each other into the front hallway and keep the rest shut. Being fully known can be frightening. Never being known at all can be lonely. Today's psalm stands right between the two. It says: you have been seen in every room, and you have not been walked out on.
screen: `A FEW LOCKED ROOMS.` → `AFRAID OF BEING KNOWN.` → `LONELY IF WE'RE NOT.`

segments.voice: The title is the older English wording: thou hast searched me. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says: "Lord, thou hast proved me, and known me." Proved, as in tested. Under both is the Hebrew chaqar, to search out, to examine through and through. First, known. The psalmist says God knows his sitting down and his rising up, understands his thoughts from far off, knows his ways before he takes them. That could sound like surveillance. It reads like wonder. Second, nowhere God is not. In the Douay-Rheims: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend into heaven, thou art there: if I descend into hell, thou art present." Up, down, the far end of the sea, the dark itself: the psalmist tries every exit and finds God already there, not to trap him but to hold him. Even darkness, he says, is not dark to you. Third, made. "Thou hast protected me from my mother's womb," the Douay says, and the psalmist marvels at how he was formed before anyone saw him. Before anyone else knew he existed, he was known. Catholics hear this psalm at Easter: the old entrance chant of Easter Sunday, Resurrexi, draws on a verse of it, I arose, and am still with thee. And the psalm ends where it started, but now as a request: prove me, O God, and know my heart. The knowing that could have been frightening becomes something he asks for.

If you pray, rest in the psalm's claim that God has already seen that room and hasn't left, and say its closing words: prove me, O God, and know my heart. If you don't, simply breathe, and let yourself be all of who you are for two minutes.

191.title: Let every spirit praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
191.hook: trumpets, harp, timbrel, cymbals, and everything that breathes
191.howItsDone: Catholics sing the Alleluia before the Gospel at Mass, omit it through Lent, and bring it back at the Easter Vigil; Psalm 150 is prayed at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thou hast searched me, chaqar: seen in every room, and still held. Your line was known, and not left. Today, the last psalm of all.

Trumpet. Psaltery and harp. Timbrel and choir. Strings and organs. High-sounding cymbals, then cymbals of joy. That's the last psalm in the book, and it reads like a finale: every player coming in at once, nobody holding anything back for later. The book of Psalms carries joy and grief, anger and trust. It ends here, every instrument sounding, and then the music handed to anyone with breath in their lungs. Today's word is the one it's built on: Alleluia.
screen: `THE LAST PSALM: A FINALE.` → `EVERY INSTRUMENT AT ONCE.` → `THEN, EVERYONE WHO BREATHES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Alleluia is Hebrew, hallelu-Yah: hallelu, all of you, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. So it isn't a feeling, it's an invitation: everybody, praise God. It came into Greek and Latin untranslated, and Catholics still sing it that way today. Second, the orchestra. Psalm 150 is six verses, and almost every line is a call to praise. It moves out from the sanctuary to the sky, then through the band. In the Douay-Rheims: "Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp." Then timbrel and choir, strings and organs, and two kinds of cymbals. Nothing is held back. Third, the last line. After all the instruments, it lands on the one everybody has: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." The Hebrew says everything that has breath; the Latin, and the Douay after it, say spirit. You don't need a trumpet. You need lungs. Fourth, how Catholics keep this word. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel at Mass. Through the whole of Lent, the Church goes without it. On Easter night, at the Vigil, it comes back, sung three times, rising each time. So the Psalms end. Over thirty-five days the path ran from the two ways of Psalm one, through the shepherd, the Miserere, the pilgrims' road, the depths and the rivers of exile, to a finale where everything that breathes is invited to join.

192.title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
192.hook: no birth story, just the beginning of the good news and a voice in the desert
192.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics stand for the Gospel, trace a small cross on forehead, lips and heart as it is announced, and hear it read by a deacon or priest; the Gospel of Mark is read on most Sundays in Year B of the lectionary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alleluia, and the Psalms ended with everything that breathes. That was your line. Today, a new book, read straight through.

Most stories about a famous person start with a birth: a baby, a family, a hometown, a childhood. Matthew and Luke do that: angels, shepherds, wise men, a stable. Mark doesn't. No manger. No star. No Mary and Joseph on the road. Mark opens with one line, like a title card at the start of a film, then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild man in camel's hair is shouting at crowds. For forty days, it's Mark start to finish, a few verses at a time. Today's word is in his first sentence: gospel.
screen: `NO MANGER. NO STAR.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE CARD.` → `FORTY DAYS OF MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole first verse. Mark says what he's writing and who it's about, and wastes no words. Second, the word. Gospel comes from old English, god-spel, good story, good news. Mark wrote in Greek, and his word is euangelion. In his world it was the word for big public news: a victory announced, a new emperor, a royal birth, sent out by messengers to every town. Greek Isaiah used the same root for heralds running ahead of God, and Paul was already using the word for the message about Jesus. Mark sets it over the whole story: this is the real headline. Third, the voice. Mark quotes the prophets: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." And there's John the Baptist, living rough in camel's hair with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, calling people to be baptized in the Jordan and turn their lives around. Crowds come from the whole countryside and from Jerusalem. Then John points away from himself: someone mightier is coming after me; I'm not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. Fourth, the book. Mark is the shortest of the four gospels. Many scholars think it was the first written, and an early tradition says Mark set down what he'd heard Peter preach. You can read it aloud in about two hours. It moves fast, as tomorrow shows.

193.title: Straight into the desert (Mark 1:9–13)
193.hook: baptism, the voice, then the Spirit drives him out among the wild beasts
193.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that closes the Christmas season, and hear Mark's short account of the forty days in the desert on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beginning of Mark, and the word gospel. Your line was gospel means good news. Today, Jesus walks into the story.

Some storytellers linger. They give you the weather, the smell of the kitchen, what everyone was wearing. Not Mark. Mark is the friend who tells a story so fast you have to say, wait, back up. In five verses today, Jesus arrives from a small village, is baptized in a river, sees the sky rip open, hears a voice, and is driven out into the wilderness for forty days. Mark has a favorite word for this speed, and you're going to start hearing it everywhere.
screen: `SOME STORYTELLERS LINGER.` → `MARK DOES NOT.` → `FIVE VERSES, FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the river. Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptizes him in the Jordan. Mark doesn't stop to explain why. He just moves. Second, the word. In the Douay-Rheims: "And forthwith coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit as a dove descending, and remaining on him." Forthwith. Older English Bibles say straightway. In Greek it's euthys, immediately, right then. Mark reaches for it again and again, and it gives his whole gospel the feeling of running. Third, the sky. Where the English says opened, Mark's Greek actually says the heavens were torn, ripped like cloth. And a voice from heaven says: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. Catholics see the whole Trinity in this moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. Fourth, the desert. Then, immediately again: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert." Drove is a strong word, the same word Mark later uses for driving out demons. Jesus is there forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serve him. Mark gives it one sentence. He doesn't tell us what the temptations were; Matthew and Luke do that. Mark leaves them untold, and adds a detail of his own: the wild beasts. Beloved, and straight into the wilderness: in Mark, being loved by God doesn't mean an easy road. It means the road starts right away.

194.title: Fishers of men (Mark 1:14–20)
194.hook: the kingdom is at hand, and fishermen leave their nets
194.howItsDone: Catholics hear the call of the first disciples at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the pope wears the Ring of the Fisherman as a sign of succession to Saint Peter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, straight into the desert, euthys: the river, the torn sky, the forty days. Your line was straightway. Today, the first followers.

A lake in Galilee. Two brothers stand in the shallows, throwing a round net out over the water, hauling it in, throwing it again. Down the shore, two more brothers sit in their father's boat, mending nets. Ordinary work, done with the hands, the same today as yesterday. Then a man walks along the beach, stops, and calls to them. Before long, all four have left that shore.
screen: `A LAKE IN GALILEE.` → `CASTING NETS, MENDING NETS.` → `A MAN WALKS ALONG THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: First, the announcement. John the Baptist has been arrested, and Jesus comes into Galilee with a message you can say in one breath. In the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." At hand means close enough to touch. Repent, in Greek metanoia, means more than feeling sorry. It means turning your mind around, facing a new way. Second, the call. Jesus sees Simon and his brother Andrew casting their nets into the sea, and says: "Come after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." He uses their own work. You catch fish; now you'll gather people. Third, the leaving, with Mark's favorite word again: "And immediately leaving their nets, they followed him." A little further on he calls James and John, the sons of Zebedee, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men and go. Notice what Mark doesn't say: whether they'd heard Jesus preach before, what they felt, what their father said. John's gospel suggests some of them had met Jesus earlier; Mark just shows the leaving. Fourth, why Catholics care. Simon is the one Jesus will call Peter, and Catholics see in him the first of the popes. A pope receives a ring called the Ring of the Fisherman, a reminder of a beach and men who dropped their nets.

195.title: A day in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–39)
195.hook: teaching, healing late into the night, and before dawn he goes out alone to pray
195.howItsDone: Catholics may begin the day with Morning Prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours or a morning offering, and in monasteries the first prayers of the day are sung before dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, halieis anthropon, fishers of men: four fishermen on a beach, and a call. Your line was they left their nets. Today, their first day together.

Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake. Mark gives one day there almost hour by hour, and it doesn't let up. Morning in the synagogue. Afternoon at Simon's house. Evening, the whole town at the door. Every hour, someone needs something. It's the kind of day that ends in the dark with no memory of lunch. And then, the next morning, before anyone is awake, a detail that shows how Jesus met a day like that.
screen: `A DAY THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `CAPERNAUM, HOUR BY HOUR.` → `AND THE NEXT MORNING.`

segments.voice: First, the morning. It's the sabbath, and Jesus teaches in the synagogue. People are astonished, Mark says, because he teaches as one having authority, and not as the scribes. Mark doesn't spell out the difference. A man with an unclean spirit cries out, and Jesus silences the spirit and sends it out. Second, the afternoon, at the house of Simon and Andrew. Simon's mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus goes to her, takes her by the hand, and lifts her up, and the fever leaves her. That small detail tells you something else: Peter had a wife. Third, the evening. Mark notes that the sun has set, and some readers connect that to the sabbath ending. The sick are brought, and the whole town gathers at the door. Mark says he healed many. Fourth, the dawn. In the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." After a day like that, before anyone's up, he slips out alone. Mark doesn't tell us what he prayed, only that he went. And they come hunting for him. Simon finds him and says, almost impatiently: "All seek for thee." Jesus doesn't go back to the crowd. Let's go on to the next towns, he says, so I can preach there too; that's why I came. In Capernaum today, pilgrims visit a house that tradition says was Peter's.

196.title: If thou wilt (Mark 1:40–45)
196.hook: a leper kneels, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him
196.howItsDone: Catholics hear the healing of the leper at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the Church honors saints who served people with leprosy, such as Francis of Assisi and Damien of Molokai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a day in Capernaum, and prayer before dawn. Your line was rising very early. Today, someone kneels.

Leviticus spells out the rule. A person with leprosy goes with clothes loose and head bare, covers the mouth, and cries out unclean, so others keep their distance. That person lives alone, outside the camp. No hand on the shoulder. No embrace at the door. In today's story, a man living under that rule walks straight up to Jesus, kneels, and says a sentence that begins with three small words.
screen: `CRYING OUT UNCLEAN.` → `ALONE, OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `A MAN KNEELS.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Under the law of Moses he's meant to keep his distance, calling out his warning. So he shouldn't be anywhere near Jesus. He comes anyway. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." He doesn't doubt Jesus can. He isn't sure Jesus wants to. Second, the touch. "And Jesus having compassion on him, stretched forth his hand; and touching him, saith to him: I will. Be thou made clean." He touches him before he heals him. He didn't need to; elsewhere Jesus heals with a word. And under the law, touching a leper made you unclean too. Jesus reaches out anyway. For a man who lived outside the camp, the touch may have been the first healing. Third, the word compassion. Mark's Greek is splanchnistheis, from the word for the inward parts: moved in the gut, a feeling from deep inside. Before he says a word, Jesus is moved. Fourth, the swap. Jesus tells the man to show himself to the priest, as Moses commanded, and to tell no one. The man tells everyone. Now Jesus can't openly enter a town, and stays out in deserted places. The man is back inside; Jesus is outside. Centuries later, Saint Francis of Assisi wrote that the Lord led him among lepers, and that what had seemed bitter was turned to sweetness; early stories say he kissed one. This week began with the psalm about being known, and ends with a hand reaching out to touch.
screen: `HE KNEELS: IF THOU WILT.` · `HE TOUCHES BEFORE HE HEALS.` · `MOVED IN THE GUT.` · `THE MAN IN, JESUS OUT.` · then, large: `I WILL. BE THOU MADE CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who doesn't get touched much, an older neighbor who lives alone, a grandparent in a care home, someone sick or grieving, a kid who's been left out, and see their face. If you pray, hold them before God and say the leper's words for them: if thou wilt. If you don't, decide how you might reach them: a hand on the arm, a hug, or a visit.
Splanchnistheis. Mark's Greek word for moved with compassion, from the gut, what Jesus felt before he touched the leper who said, if thou wilt. Today's word.
Your line: he touched him. The week ran from thou hast searched me and Alleluia into Mark: the gospel, the desert, the nets, Capernaum, and now a touch. Day one hundred ninety-six, done.
